amendments.summary: Kerala has not amended Section 138 (or ss.139-147) of the Negotiable Instruments Act - the offence, the presumptions, the notice period and limitation, and compounding are uniform central law, and Kerala adds nothing to that statute. What sits here instead are Kerala's own State Acts that bear on a s.138 case - chiefly the Kerala Police Act, 2011, which governs who serves process and executes the court's warrants. Also here is the Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, whose Article 21 fixes the court fee on a §138 complaint, appeal and revision. The rules of practice and e-filing rules are under State rules.

items.title: Kerala Police Act, 2011
items.note: A Kerala State Act - the police machinery a s.138 case relies on at the execution stage. A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case with no police investigation and no arrest at the outset; the police enter only when the court issues process, when the local Station House Officer executes a bailable or non-bailable warrant and serves court process. Rendered from the official clean text of the Act.

key.label: Functions of the police
key.note: The general duty of the police to serve court process and execute warrants - the point at which the police enter a s.138 case. There is no police investigation or arrest at the outset; they act only on the court's process once it issues.

items.title: Kerala Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1959
items.cite: State Act · court fees on a §138 case
items.note: The State Act that fixes what it costs to bring and contest a cheque case in Kerala. The Kerala Finance Act, 2024 inserted Article 21 into Schedule II, setting the court fee on a §138 complaint (₹250 where the cheque is ≤ ₹10,000; otherwise 5% of the cheque amount, capped at ₹3 lakh), on an appeal (₹1,000 for the accused to the Sessions Court; half the trial-court fee for the complainant to the High Court) and on a revision (one-tenth of the cheque amount, or ₹1,500 for the accused). The slabs were revised again by the Finance Act, 2025 - verify the current figure before relying on it.

key.label: Court fee on a §138 complaint, appeal & revision
key.note: The ad valorem court fee that prices every stage of a Kerala cheque case - complaint, appeal and revision - scaled to the dishonoured-cheque amount. This is the filing economics a complainant meets before the case even begins.

edges.rel: sets the fee to file a complaint under
priced on the complaint taken under

rules.summary: How a Section 138 case is actually filed and tried in Kerala - the rules of practice and procedure a High Court or the State makes for its own courts (subsidiary legislation, made under an enabling Act). These sit on top of the uniform central offence and govern the form of process, service and the warrant ladder.

items.title: Criminal Rules of Practice, Kerala, 1982
items.note: The core state instrument for how a criminal court in Kerala signs, forms and serves process. Rules 7 to 14 cover summons to the accused and witnesses (police officers are summoned through their superior officer); Rule 13 sets the form; Rule 14 requires an English translation of process issued in Malayalam. Chapter III carries the absconding-accused track, and the Rules carry the forms and mechanics for warrants and for proclamation and attachment.

key.label: Signing & issue of summons
key.note: Who signs the summons to the accused and witnesses, and in whose name - the local mechanics behind issuing process on a s.138 complaint.

key.label: Form of summons
key.note: Prescribes the form the summons takes.

key.label: Translation of process
key.note: Process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation - the court-language rule biting on every summons and notice a s.138 case generates.

key.label: Absconding accused - proclamation & attachment
key.note: The warrant/absconder track: what the court does when the accused does not answer summons, escalating to proclamation and attachment of property - the far end of the summons -> warrant ladder in a s.138 case.

items.title: Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971
items.note: Govern the High Court's own side: appeals, revisions and criminal miscellaneous petitions, including quashing a s.138 complaint under s.482 CrPC / s.528 BNSS or a revision against conviction. A large share of Kerala s.138 litigation is the quashing and revision layer at the High Court.

key.label: Revision petitions
key.note: How a revision reaches the High Court - the route for a s.138 conviction or acquittal to be re-examined.

key.label: Procedure in criminal matters
key.note: The High Court's criminal-side procedure, including the quashing petitions under which many s.138 complaints are challenged.

items.title: Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala), 2021
items.note: The enabling rules for e-filing a complaint in Kerala courts. These govern how a s.138 complaint is filed, not how summons or warrants are served electronically.

key.label: Scope & applicability
key.note: Which courts and filings the e-filing regime covers - the gateway a s.138 complaint passes through when filed electronically.

key.label: Service through electronic means
key.note: When service by electronic means is permitted under the e-filing regime - the state's answer sits alongside the statutory modes of serving the demand notice and summons.

notifications.summary: Government orders, special-court notifications and standard operating procedures that shape how a §138 case is set up and run in Kerala - including the Kollam pilot court itself.

items.title: Special §138 Court at Kollam - 24×7 ON Court, 2024
items.note: The notification that stood up the Kollam pilot court itself. Issued under the proviso to section 9(1) BNSS and in consultation with the High Court, it establishes a dedicated Special Judicial Magistrate of the First Class at Kollam to try only §138 cheque cases, running as India's first 24×7 digital 'ON Court', with effect from 20 November 2024 (earlier sanctioned by G.O. 21/2024/Home dated 19 October 2024). This is the on-the-ground court the whole Kerala layer describes.

key.label: Establishment of the §138 Special Court (24×7 ON Court)
key.note: Creates a dedicated JMFC at Kollam to try only §138 cases as a 24×7 digital court, w.e.f. 20 November 2024. It is the court that hears the cheque case the rest of this layer feeds into - a concrete implementation of the summary-trial and special-court push for expeditious §138 disposal.

items.title: SOP for e-Filing in the District Judiciary through the DCMS portal
items.note: The current operating procedure for filing a complaint through the DCMS portal at filing.keralacourts.in. Source PDF only; not yet converted to structured text.

vocabulary.summary: The words the Kerala layer adds on top of the shared national vocabulary - the court officers, records, process and filing terms a s.138 case actually runs on in Kerala. (Terms drawn from the field - how people on the ground name things - will be added here as the Local practice layer is built.)

terms.gloss: The court officer who, 'by order of the Court', ordinarily signs and issues the summons to the accused and witnesses in a Kerala criminal court.
The prescribed words that must precede the ministerial officer's signature on a summons.
The court's running administrative record of a case (Administrative Form No. 10).
The sheet on which the day-to-day proceedings of a case are recorded (Judicial Form No. 61).
The officer in charge of a police station; in a s.138 case the person who executes the court's warrant and serves its process - the only point at which the police enter the case.
terms.source: Kerala Police Act, §4 (functions of the police)
aka: officer in charge of the police station

terms.gloss: The statutory duties of the Kerala police, including serving court process and executing warrants - a s.138 case is a complaint case, so the police act only on the court's process, never by investigation.
Court process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation - the point where the court-language rule bites on a summons or notice.
The working language of Kerala's subordinate courts; it shapes the summons, the demand-notice evidence, orders and the filing interface a s.138 case passes through.
The District Court Case Management System at filing.keralacourts.in through which a s.138 complaint is electronically filed in Kerala.
When the Kerala e-filing regime permits service by electronic means - narrower than informal WhatsApp/e-mail service, which the High Court has declined to sanction (Anoop Jacob).
Kollam's dedicated §138 court, running round-the-clock as India's first fully digital 'ON Court' - the concrete court the Kerala layer describes.
A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class court set up under the proviso to section 9(1) BNSS to try only cheque-bounce cases - Kerala's sits at Kollam.

The ad valorem fee to file a cheque complaint in Kerala - ₹250 up to a ₹10,000 cheque, otherwise 5% of the cheque amount capped at ₹3 lakh (Article 21, Court Fees Act; revised by the Finance Act 2025).
The clerk who attends the sitting - calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper.
Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment; the depositions are headed and signed as the rules prescribe.
Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which in Kerala is Malayalam; put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret.
A person who stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance; the court tests the surety's sufficiency.
Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry - a recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
terms.source: Court-precinct and registry practice (not a statutory office)

terms.gloss: How the national Oaths Act, 1969 requirement is run on the ground in Kerala: the Criminal Rules of Practice name the officer who administers the oath (Rule 50) and prescribe its form (Rule 51). A witness, interpreter or deponent is bound by it before giving evidence; one who objects to being sworn makes a solemn affirmation instead.

The document by which a party authorises an advocate to appear and act for them; until it is on record the advocate has no authority to represent the party. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe its form and attestation (Rule 32).

A witness's evidence as recorded in court and signed. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe how depositions are headed (Rule 56) and signed (Rule 57); in a summary §138 trial much of the evidence reaches the record as affidavits rather than long oral depositions.

The rules the High Court of Kerala made in 1982, under Article 227 of the Constitution, to govern how the criminal courts below it actually run - filing, the court diary, oaths, depositions, the vakalatnama, bail and so on. This site cites them as the source of most of the Kerala state-layer vocabulary.

The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises and notes objections (E-Filing Rules r.17); a defective petition is not numbered and is returned for amendment and representation (CRP r.68). 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules name 'the Registry' or the 'officer concerned', not this title.
terms.source: E-Filing Rules, Kerala, r.17 (read with CRP r.68)

informal.title: the title is functional, not a titled post in the rules
informal.practice: reported holding of files for payment (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified)

terms.gloss: The court's administrative office - the ministerial establishment that receives filings, scrutinises them for defects, numbers and lists the case, keeps the records and issues process. A s.138 complaint is presented here before it reaches the Magistrate: the office checks the form and enclosures under the Criminal Rules of Practice (rule 27 on presentation of proceedings; rule 68 on returning defective petitions), and on e-filing the Electronic Filing Rules assign the same scrutiny to 'the Registry'. In the High Court the office is headed by the Registrar under the Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971.

The formal written statements in which each side sets out its case on paper. In a s.138 prosecution the pleadings are the complaint with its annexures and the accused's reply or defence; the Electronic Filing Rules speak of scrutinising and storing 'the pleadings and documents' filed in a case (rules 14 and 15). The classic definition comes from the Code of Civil Procedure, Order VI - a plaint or a written statement - and the usage carries over into criminal filing practice.
terms.source: Electronic Filing Rules for Courts (Kerala), Rule 14

terms.gloss: The relief clause of a petition or complaint - the specific order the party asks the court to pass, usually set out and numbered at the end of the document. In a s.138 complaint the prayer is to take cognizance and try the accused, and on conviction to award a fine or compensation to the payee. It has no separate defining rule; the convention comes from the Code of Civil Procedure, Order VII rule 7, which requires a plaint to state the relief claimed, and drafting practice carries it into criminal petitions.
terms.source: Court drafting practice (cf. CPC Order VII rule 7)

story.summary: How a §138 cheque-bounce case runs in Kerala, from filing to disposal - built purely from the rules and Acts, with every step citing the provision that governs it. Click any citation to open the exact text. This is the de jure process the black-letter rules prescribe; the lived, local practice is a separate layer.

process.summary: The procedural spine is the uniform national code (BNSS + the NI Act); Kerala's own rules operationalise each step. Where Kerala adds nothing, the step is pure central law.

timing.prescribed: Within 1 month of cause of action

steps.t: A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case: the payee or holder in due course files a written complaint, and the Magistrate can take cognizance only on such a complaint (never on a police report).
It must be filed within one month of the cause of action - which arises when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the demand notice served after dishonour.
In Kerala the complaint is e-filed through the DCMS portal under the E-Filing Rules, and the court fee is paid on filing.

timing.regular: Days to a couple of weeks
timing.oncourt: Same day; e-scrutiny by the Registry

steps.t: Before the complaint is numbered and placed for cognizance it is scrutinised for defects. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises the pleadings and documents and notes objections; a defective petition is not numbered and is returned to the party, pleader or officer concerned for amendment and representation.

On the ground this is done by an official commonly called the scrutiny officer. Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward. The scrutiny function is in the rules; the title and this practice are not.
The Magistrate examines the complainant (and any witnesses) on oath and, if satisfied there is ground to proceed, takes cognizance and issues process to the accused.
The summons is signed and issued by the court's ministerial officer 'by order of the Court', in the prescribed form.
Because the court language is Malayalam, process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation.
The summons is served in the manner the BNSS prescribes, and the NI Act's own mode of service also applies.
Service is effected through the police - the local Station House Officer serves the court's process. This is the only point at which the police enter a §138 case.
Where the e-filing regime permits, service may be by electronic means.

stages.stage: 4 · If the accused does not appear

steps.t: The court escalates up the warrant ladder: a warrant issues, and on continued absconding, proclamation and attachment of property.
Kerala's rules carry the absconding-accused track; the police execute the warrant.
The case is tried summarily, and the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit - the features that make §138 a fast-track offence.
A presumption operates in favour of the holder that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability, unless the accused rebuts it.
Kerala adds nothing procedural here - the summary-trial machinery is uniform central law.
On conviction the court may impose imprisonment up to two years and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, with compensation to the complainant.
The offence is compoundable: the parties may settle at any stage and the case is compounded, ending the prosecution.
The accused may appeal; the appellate court may require a deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine/compensation as a condition of the appeal.
A revision lies to the High Court, whose own rules govern its criminal side.
A complaint may also be challenged by a quashing petition before the High Court.

process.timing_note: Prescribed shows the statutory or rule deadline where one exists. The Regular court and ON Court columns are indicative typical durations shown for illustration, not official statistics; actual timelines vary case to case.

fees.summary: What it costs to bring and contest a §138 case in Kerala - the ad valorem court fee scaled to the dishonoured-cheque amount, set by Article 21 of the Court Fees Act (inserted by the Finance Act 2024).

items.fee: ₹250 where the cheque is ≤ ₹10,000; otherwise 5% of the cheque amount, capped at ₹3 lakh.
One-half of the court fee paid in the trial court (appeal to the High Court).
One-tenth of the cheque amount (challenging insufficiency of sentence).

fees.note: Figures are the 2024 schedule; the Kerala Finance Act 2025 revised the slabs - verify the current figure before relying on it.

courts.summary: The rules designate exactly one court specifically for §138 in Kerala - the Kollam 24×7 ON Court. Everywhere else, ordinary Judicial First Class Magistrate courts hear §138 cases under their general criminal jurisdiction; a full statewide list is external court-establishment data, shown as a placeholder below.

designated.basis: India's first fully digital, round-the-clock court, dedicated to §138 cases, w.e.f. 20 Nov 2024.

roles.summary: Who does what in a §138 case - the parties, their lawyers, the magistrate, and the court and police staff - and the provision each role is drawn from. Click a citation to read the source.

items.who: The payee or the holder in due course of the dishonoured cheque. Only this person can set a §138 case going, by filing the complaint in their own name.

Where duly authorised and personally aware of the transaction, may file the complaint and depose on the complainant's behalf - a point the Supreme Court has settled for §138 cases. Stands in the payee's place, not as a separate party.
The drawer of the cheque, prosecuted for the dishonour. Where the drawer is a company, the company and every person who was in charge of and responsible to it.
Stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance. The court tests the surety's sufficiency before accepting the bond.
The bank on which the cheque is drawn. Its return of the cheque unpaid is the event the offence turns on, and its return memo proves both the dishonour and the reason for it.
Gives evidence on the facts. In a §138 case the complainant's evidence may be led on affidavit, and an officer of the drawee bank often proves the dishonour. A witness is sworn before deposing.
The legal practitioner who appears for the complainant or the accused. The right to appear flows from enrolment under the Advocates Act.
Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry. A recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
items.basis: Court-precinct and registry practice, governed by the High Court's rules rather than a provision of the substantive law.

items.who: The Judicial Magistrate of the First Class who takes cognizance of the complaint, tries it summarily and passes judgment. In Kerala a §138 case may be assigned to the designated Special Court.
The court's senior ministerial officer who signs and issues the summons and other process 'by order of the Court'.
The clerk who attends the sitting: calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper - the running record of each hearing.
Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment. The depositions they record are headed and signed in the form the rules prescribe.

Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which matters in Kerala where the court language is Malayalam. The interpreter is put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret the evidence.
The local police officer who executes warrants and serves the process the court issues, as part of the statutory functions of the police.

The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance, noting objections or returning it for amendment.

informal.title: 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules assign scrutiny to 'the Registry' (E-Filing Rules r.17) and returns to the 'officer concerned' (CRP r.68).
informal.practice: Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward.
